item.title: Want a better winter workout? Train your muscle clocks
item.description:
TikTok has another trend: the winter arc. It’s a self-improvement challenge where people try to be their best self in the 3 months leading up to New Year – often, through exercise. We at Short Wave wanted to know if the science really holds up: Is ramping up your exercise routine when your circadian rhythm may be struggling with less light really a good idea? So we called up NPR health correspondent, Will Stone. He’s done a deep dive on what scientists do and don’t know about exercise and our circadian rhythms.

To read more of Will’s reporting on creating a solid exercise routine.

If you liked this episode, check out our episodes on “circadian depression”, and the science of jet lag and how to avoid it.

item.title: Windows Server 2028 removes 32bit application support
item.description: Windows Server 2028 is going to make more drastic changes than just hardening its core, it turns out. Microsoft has announced that it’s removing the app compatibility layer that allows 32-bit Windows apps to run on 64-bit installs of the OS with the next version of Windows Sever, officially labeled Windows Server 2028. For the first time, the OS will not ship by default with the WoW64 compatibility later that enabled 32-bit apps to run on 64-bit Windows. The last 32-bit version of Windows Server shipped in 2008, with all subsequent releases being 64-bit only. The WoW64 subsystem shipped on 64-bit Windows to allow 32-bit Windows apps to continue running on 64-bit versions of Windows. But now, with Windows Server 2028, that 32-bit compatibility layer will now be an optional component that you can install manually if needed. ↫ Zac Bowden at Windows Central You can still install the WoW64 layer if you wish to do so, but by default, it won’t be installed. Now, there’s no indication that this will spill over into the client versions of Windows 11 any time soon, but it wouldn’t be the first time that Windows Server ends up serving as a testbed for the future of client releases. Perhaps WoW64 becomes something you can optionally remove, but I honestly doubt Microsoft is ready yet to cut 32bit support from Windows 11 by default. Regardless, this is an interesting development and I would love to be able to cut the entirety of 32bit support from Windows 11.

item.title: NixOS bring-up on an Alibaba RISC-V board
item.description: For certain reasons, I’m in a mood to highlight as many more alternative ways to do the computers things than just the boring Windows/Linux+x86 thing. In the process of scouring Alibaba for a cheap Versal devkit, I unexpectedly came into possession of a Zhihe Computing A210 RISC-V SoC. It’s a cool board: there’s a ridiculous amount of IO exposed by the baseboard, not to mention 8 cores clocked at 1.9 GHz is nothing to sniff at for a RISC-V CPU. I’m not sure I could recommend buying any RISC-V SoC currently, but all these distros that are starting to support RISC-V need to run tests somewhere that isn’t Spike/QEMU. I decided to make this board into a NixOS build server so I could learn more about the state of RISC-V support in NixOS and to get some practice in Linux bringup. ↫ George Huebner I will not create a NixOS category.

item.title: Windows Server 2028 enters public preview with hardened Server Core by default
item.description: Microsoft has announced the public preview of Window Server 2028, and of course, the announcement is a useless jumble of buzzwords and slop, so I’m not going to spend any time decoding it. However, there is one major change coming in Server 2028 that everyone working with this platform really ought to be aware of – a massive hardening of Server Core that will definitely break things that used to work fine on Server 2025. It even got its own detailed blog post that’s a lot more interesting than the actual public preview announcement. Up to and including Windows Server 2025, a stock installation was insecure, unhardened by default, with the expectation and norm being that administrators applied their own hardening scripts and settings post-installation. With Server 2028, that’s changing, and Server Core will now be secured and hardened out of the box, with administrators having to explicitly relax any settings their workloads might require. Starting with Windows Server Insider Preview build 29706, Server Core installs hardened. Hundreds of security settings are on from first boot. They’re aligned with the industry benchmarks you’re already measured against, such as CIS and DISA STIG. The secure configuration is the starting state, not a project you run after setup. That closes the window where a newly deployed server sits exposed while it waits to be hardened. ↫ Christina Curlette Things like identity and authentication, cryptography, privilege and admin access, remote access, and more, are all locked down and use only the most up-to-date features, cyphers, best practices, and so on. I’m no system administrator, but it seems kind of wild to me that this hasn’t always been the norm. I’m glad they’re at least moving to it now, starting with Insider Preview build 29706

item.title: Microsoft is finally upgrading Windows 11’s default PowerShell to version 7.x
item.description: In true Microsoft fashion, the version of PowerShell that ships with every Windows installation is not the latest version of PowerShell. Even if you fully update your Windows 11 installation, including all of its applications, you’ll still be stuck on an old version of PowerShell. While a fully updated Windows 11 installation has version 5.1, the most recent version is actually PowerShell 7.7. What makes matters worse is that PowerShell 5.1 hasn’t seen any significant development in ten years, only receiving security updates, with all development work focusing on PowerShell 7 for years now. Well, all of this is finally about to change, as the next version of Windows 11 – whatever that may be, Microsoft won’t say – will ship with PowerShell 7.x instead of 5.1. PowerShell 7 is coming to Windows. Beginning with the next release of Windows, PowerShell 7 will be included as the upgrade for Windows PowerShell 5.1. The Windows team has published the details in KB5137172. Here is what this means for you, your scripts, your automation, and where our work stands. ↫ Jason Helmick at Microsoft’s Dev Blog Microsoft also explains why it’s taken this long. The problem is that a lot of scripts, services, and mor rely on PowerShell 5.1, and PowerShell 7’s backwards compatibility wasn’t up to Microsoft’s strict standards on this front for years. Apparently, PowerShell 7.7 is now at a point where Microsoft feels comfortable moving everyone over to it by default. It seems that the only remaining issues stem from the fact that PowerShell 7 is delivered as an MSIX package as opposed to an MSI installer, and this brings some problems with it, which Microsoft is tracking on GitHub. Of course, you can already install and switch to PowerShell 7.x today if you want to, without losing access to PowerShell 5.1, as the two shell versions can live alongside each other.

item.title: How a viral video gave a huge boost to new gene therapy
item.description:
Sanfilippo syndrome is a rare and degenerative disease that can be fatal by the time someone reaches their teens. So the O’Neill family knew they didn’t have much time after learning their 4-year old daughter, Eliza, had it. At the time no treatment existed, and the world of drug development had its eyes on more common illnesses. So the family took an all hands on deck, unusual approach to directly raise money and boost medical research. NPR pharmaceutical correspondent Sydney Lupkin shares what happened next, and what she learned from the O’Neills story about the promises and challenges of drug development.

item.title: Finally, a truly premium Linux laptop: Star Labs’ StarFighter Ultra
item.description: Many popular Linux laptops are not designed from the ground-up for Linux. Often, they are machines designed and assembled by companies like Clevo, with parts and options picked by the Linux OEM to optimise them for Linux to make sure the hardware is optimally compatible. While there’s nothing wrong with this approach – there are countless great Linux laptops available that are made this way – there’s also something to be said for starting with a blank slate, and designing, developing, building, and assembling a Linux laptop entirely from scratch. One such laptop is Star Labs’ brand new StarFighter, which I’ve been using and testing over the last little while since it was launched. The StarFighter is an entirely custom powerhouse of a laptop, designed exclusively for Linux, both inside and out. Let’s talk about what it’s like to use the StarFighter, and if it’s worth considering when looking for a new laptop. The hardware The Starfighter comes in three flavours: Standard, Ultra, and AMD. I opted for the Ultra model, which comes with an Intel Core Ultra 9 285H, an Intel Arc 140T integrated GPU, 64GB of LPDDR5X RAM, and a 16″ 3840×2400 120Hz matte display. The standard model steps these specs down to an Intel Core Ultra 5 125H, 32GB of LPDDR5X RAM, and a 16″ 2560×1600 165Hz display, while the AMD model maintains the specifications of the Ultra, but with an AMD Ryzen 7 8845HS processor paired with a Radeon 780M integrated GPU. All three models share the same Intel AX210 Wi-Fi 6E chip, soldered RAM, and port configuration: 2 USB-C ports (Thunderbolt 4 on the Intel models), 3 USB-A ports, an HDMI 2.0 port, a microSD reader, a combined audio jack, and two PCIe Gen 4 NVMe slots on the motherboard. All three models run coreboot firmware, and come with a hardware kill switch for the wireless radios. Another really interesting security and privacy feature is how the Starfighter handles its webcam. Instead of being integrated into the display bezel, the webcam is a separate module that snaps onto the display lid magnetically, connecting through a few pogo pins (which form a USB 2.0 port, which I’m sure intrepid hardware hackers could do fun stuff with). When not in use, the webcam module is stored in its own little metal tray that slides out of the side of the laptop, securing itself in place magnetically. Neat. The webcam quality itself is decidedly average. I personally don’t ever use a webcam, but if you do, don’t expect miracles. It does its job, no more, no less. The StarFighter has a custom chassis made out of magnesium, with the only plastic part of the casing being the display inner hinge cover where I assume the antennas are integrated. It’s an incredibly sturdy device, with very little flex in the display cover, and zero flex in the keyboard deck. Thanks to the properties of magnesium, it’s quite lightweight at a mere 1.6kg. The bottom cover is easily removable, but the two screws in the middle of that cover are ever so slightly longer than all the other screws – ask me how I know. Star Labs opted for an understated, unobtrusive design. There’s no weird flourishes, no garish RGB lighting, no childish font on the keyboard – it’s all business, and I really like that. The dark finish feels incredibly nice, and despite the colour doesn’t seem to catch too many fingerprints. The speaker grills next to the keyboard look nice too, as does the keyboard itself – I especially appreciate that the the various modifier and non-character keys use text labels instead of symbols. Of course, since this is a Linux laptop, the super key is properly labelled. No Windows logo here, but no silly penguin either. The keyboard is backlit, of course, with several light levels, with a keyboard backlight timeout adjustable in coreboot. Using it The feel of the keyboard could use some work, however, at least for me. In particular, the key stability feels a bit off to me, meaning that unless you strike a key right in the middle, it might not register properly, as the keys wobble more than I would expect. A workaround, of sorts, is to strike the keys a bit harder than you normally would, but I’ve found this to be more difficult to adapt to than I initially expected. That being said, if you already have a more solid strike, it’s possible you won’t notice anything wrong with the keyboard at all. The trackpad, though, is basically perfect. Star Labs pulled out all the stops here, and went for a large haptic trackpad that feels absolutely incredible. I greatly prefer haptic trackpads, and have been puzzled for years now why Linux laptop OEMs continue to opt for wobbly diving board-style trackpads instead. It has a glass surface which hits the perfect middle-ground between smooth and textured, and it never seems to pick up any smudges or grease. Several of the parameters of the haptic trackpad can be configured in coreboot and supposedly from within Linux itself, but I haven’t figured that part out yet as the patches for it were only accepted very recently. It is the perfect trackpad. Zero complaints. Every single click, every single gesture, every single swoosh feels perfect. I don’t like being this ecstatic about something – there’s usually flaws in everything – but it’s really just that good. While testing the StarFighter, I used some other laptops with the old diving board design, and they’re all ruined for me now. I’m usually a fan of smaller laptops, with 14″ being my upper bound. However, laptops have gotten so light, and bezels so thin, that the 16″ of today is the 14″ of several years ago – not exactly, but you get my point. I definitely had to get used to this larger laptop, but now that I have acclimatised, having 3840×2400 pixels spread out across a 16″ canvas is honestly kind of amazing. I

item.title: Are your body clocks off? Meet ‘circadian depression’
item.description:
What if depression is sometimes linked to your body’s internal sense of time? That’s what researchers from the University of Sydney’s Brain and Mind Centre wanted to know. In a new study, they surveyed patients with depression whose symptoms may reflect problems with their circadian rhythms – like their sleep schedule, how tired they feel in the morning and whether they’re a night owl. They found that about 1 in 4 qualified for what might be termed a circadian subtype of depression. And while there’s still a lot of research to be done, this could open up new pathways for mental health treatment. NPR health correspondent Will Stone walks us through the study and its implications.

item.title: KDE will now load XWayland on demand
item.description: When running KDE, the X11 compatibility layer for Wayland, XWayland, always runs, even if there isn’t anything on the system still requiring the legacy X server to work. In the next step towards a Wayland-only world, the KDE people have reached a major milestone: XWayland now only runs when actually needed. This week a significant technical milestone was achieved: the XWayland compatibility layer is now loaded only when needed. Previously it had always been running even when no apps were using it, and fixing this required porting various system services away from legacy X11 code paths. This work was done by Vlad Zahorodnii, David Edmundson, and David Redondo, and will ship in Plasma 6.9. ↫ Nate Graham This frees up some system resources, which is always a welcome improvement. I do wonder how this might impact the load times of legacy X applications, but I have a feeling it’s close to immeasurable.

item.title: Redox gets Go, GIMP, and more
item.description: I love and admire the Redox project, but their insistence on fudging the publication dates of their monthly progress reports really bothers me, for some reason. No, I’m not 16 days late – the report covering October was published only yesterday evening, and not on 31 October as the website claims. None of this matters to anyone but weird people such as myself, but I still want to get it off my chest. Don’t bother any Redox people about this. Anyway, the big news for the month of October is the port of the official Go programming language compiler, allowing for cross-compilation and self-hosted compilation using relibc. Another major port also made its way to Redox in October: GIMP now runs on Redox, using the Orbital backend of the GTK port. The work to make Redox compatible with Cloud Hypervisor is also complete, with more information in its own dedicated article. Video playback in WebKitGTK3 has been fixed as well, and even YouTube works now which is quite neat. There’s a ton more in this report, like an updated Servo port, NUMA support has been tested on real hardware for the first time and seems to work, work on rootless package installation has begun, and much more.

item.title: Creating a self-booting ZIP archive
item.description: Linux initramfs supports unpacking CPIO, a stupid, simple, standardized format. In the discussion on whether to support TAR instead, much emphasize has been put on the fact that CPIO is standardized and less fragmented. Luckily, Linux (the kernel) includes its own tool to produce the specific variant of the standard that it happens to implement. The standard CPIO tool is possibly the most cursed archiver under the SUN. In the old DOS/WinDOS world, ZIP was probably the most widespread and well-known archive format, being displaced to some extent by the rise of RAR during the 2000s. Because of the design of the format, ZIP lends itself to all kinds of polyglot trickery. Way back when, self extracting ZIP archives where a thing, EXE/ZIP polyglots that can be run and unpack themselves, which is useful if you don’t have an archiver installed. I don’t think I need to explain where I am going with this. ↫ David Oberhollenzer This is lovingly cursed.

item.title: AI could help hospitals diagnose PTSD in real time
item.description:
Every year, millions of people in the United States develop PTSD from a traumatic event—like a car crash, an assault or freak accident. A lot of those people end up in the ER answering the same question: “What brought you to the emergency department today?” Now, a research team in New York has an AI model that can use patients’ answers and demographics to spit out one number that tells medical staff how likely a patient is to develop PTSD a month later.

The work – published in the journal Nature Communications – could help an often-overloaded emergency department team prevent mental health disorders before they start.

item.description: The ReactOS project organised two hackfests this year, and the work done during those in-person sessions, combined with the ongoing regular progress, has led to some pretty significant breakthroughs and progress. More NT6+ syscalls have been added, ReactOS supports floppy disks now, NTFS support has been vastly improved, and much more. There’s also a new USB3/4 stack, which is now merged and offers basic support for these versions of USB. One of the biggest additions is a new kernel shim engine which gives ReactOS the ability to work around buggy drivers and implement quirks, moreso than even Windows itself can. For instance, thanks to this new shim, XP-era NVIDIA drivers can run on NT6 ReactOS. The ongoing efforts to implement SMP are yielding results too: ReactOS can now run with SMP for days on end while doing tasks in the background, which is quite promising. The team is showing off Steam and the game Among Us running on ReactOS, which is definitely impressive.

item.title: IBM to offer access to a dual-processor quantum system in 2027
item.description: Ars Technica published a short write-up about changes to IBM’s quantum computing plans. The changes greatly expand the scope of its next-generation Nighthawk general-use processors by adding a version with over 500 programmable qubits. At the same time, it’s stepping back a bit on its plan to link multiple Nighthawk processors together, dropping the intended number of linked systems from nine to two. The total number of qubits planned for next year will remain the same; how the company is getting there, however, will be different. Meanwhile, the company is touting the performance boost achieved via a major change that was made in the generation of Nighthawk processors released in September: hardware-based qubit resets. ↫ John Timmer at Ars Technica I’m convinced quantum computing will eventually have a big impact in the areas its characteristics are presumed to be well-suited for. Also, it just looks and sounds incredibly cool, even if as the technology currently stands it’s not particularly useful yet.

item.title: I’m not descending into madness because mount and unmount icons make no sense
item.description: There are many problems in this world – some big, some small, some so minute nobody ought to put them to paper at all. The problem I’m going to highlight here is even smaller than that. This literally – the actual literally – does not matter and absolutely nobody should care about it, let alone put any work into changing it or addressing it some other way. I want to talk about the iconography GNOME’s Disks utility uses to symbolise “mount” and “unmount”. No, I’m not descending into madness. GNOME’s Disks utility uses the “play” symbol on the mount button, and the “stop” symbol on the unmount button. Inexplicably, considering the state of the world in general and the rapidly deteriorating quality of software specifically, this bothers me. Out in the real world, built on decades of consistent use, these symbols have gained clearly defined meanings, and mounting and unmounting disks definitely isn’t one of them. In fact, the meaning of these symbols isn’t mere convention; they’re defined in a variety of international standards for symbols for use in software and on equipment, such as ISO/IEC 18035 (which you need to buy to read; my copy fell of a truck): ISO/IEC 18035:2002 defines a consistent set of icons and related functions that are represented by multimedia applications on a computer screen and that users interact with to control such applications. It describes controls applying to such functions as: Play, Pause, Stop, Rewind, Scan forward, Scan backward, Replay backward, Loop, Go to beginning, Go to previous, Go to next, Go to end, Set volume and Mute. ↫ ISO/IEC 18035:2003 They’re also part of ISO 7000/IEC 60417, a much larger, more encompassing standard that also contains things like the various symbols used on laundry machines, tumble dryers, in cars, and so on. The symbols themselves are much older than the standards, of course, with many of them dating back to the 1960s and possibly even 1950s. The point remains, though: the play and stop symbols have clearly defined meanings, and I don’t think they are at all a good fit for mount and unmount. The function of the “play” symbol according to ISO/IEC 18035: To enable the user to start the presentation of dynamic media, except where the task requires automatic playing of that media. ↫ ISO/IEC 18035:2003 And of the “stop” symbol: To enable the user to stop the presentation of dynamic media. ↫ ISO/IEC 18035:2003 Neither of these descriptions match what mounting and unmounting mean or do. Mounting a drive or partition doesn’t present any media at all; it merely makes the drive or partition in question accessible. Unmounting also doesn’t eject anything; it merely makes the drive or partition inaccessible. I would argue that play and pause act upon contents of a drive or volume, and not upon the drive or volume itself. As it stands right now, you “play” a drive” to “play” a video stored on said drive. Madness. I already know what you’re thinking, and yes, I agree that the Disks utility is a tool aimed at more advanced use cases and users, and most normal, average users will never even know it exists, let alone open it at all. Very few people get to see these symbols, and those that do already know full well what mounting and unmounting mean, reducing the importance of said symbols considerably. But now it’s time for the big surprise, the twist in the story that turns this entire thing on its head. Files, GNOME’s file manager, uses an entirely different symbol for unmounting! Instead of the “stop” symbol, Files uses the “eject” symbol. You may think this is a more accurate visual representation of what unmounting means, but I strongly disagree. Let’s turn to ISO/IEC 18035:2003 once again: To enable the user to eject the current physical media from the appropriate drive. ↫ ISO/IEC 18035:2003 Unmounting doesn’t eject anything! If you unmount a USB stick, the stick doesn’t get fired out of the USB port. If you unmount a volume, it doesn’t get removed from the SSD. Hell, if you unmount a CD-ROM, it doesn’t even eject it! Ejecting a CD-ROM – opening the drive’s tray or spitting the CD-ROM out of a slot-loader – is an entirely different act! Are we really “ejecting” a CD-ROM twice? Are we “mounting” a CD-ROM when we merely close the tray? No! Madness! The real underlying problem here is, of course, that mounting and unmounting are deeply weird and confusing concepts, bordering on the esoteric, that simply do not have physical equivalents to fall back on. Using symbols and iconography designed in the 1960s explicitly for playing music or stopping a video or ejecting a cassette tape are not a good fit for something as difficult to explain to most people as mounting and unmounting. It’s like putting an eject symbol on a car’s door handle or a play symbol on a soap dispenser. Should GNOME developers waste any time or resources to address this? No, of course not, that would be stupid. Nobody should care about this but me. I should suffer in silence, every time I need to mount or unmount something, forced to look for an eject or stop symbol in whatever user interface I happen to be using. Every time, I should die a little inside. Please, don’t be like me and waste precious resources thinking about this. I’m not descending into madness. I just want mount and unmount symbols that make sense. I’m not descending into madness.

item.description: An interesting question, and a detailed technical rundown of how to make this happen, which involved building a custom Linux kernel, of course. I really, really enjoy the conclusion. And you know? It turned out fine. Nothing exploded on my system. As I could predict, because this was otherwise impossible, nobody did it. The signal system was setup in such a way that you would most likely realize something you were doing was wrong, and not try it. To pull back further, it is interesting to notice how the rules we all take for granted are just set somewhere in code. They were written by someone, at some point. If there is code restricting you from doing something, someone wrote it. Either they did not think anyone would want to do that thing, or they specifically prevented you from doing it. Those rules are written somewhere, and you can take it in your paws to go sniff around the code, pull out the relevant parts, and hack around the things that bother you. For fun, learning, or convenience. Snoop around. Sniff code. Put your paws in it. item.title: Can scientists reverse your age?
item.description:
Reversing aging may sound like science fiction, but scientists have already found a way to do it—at least, theoretically. Based on a 2012 Nobel-prize winning discovery, researchers are testing whether they can revert diseased cells in the eye back to young and healthy ones. They gave people a drug this year. If it works, it’ll open the door to curing and possibly preventing other age-related diseases. And that led producer Berly McCoy to wonder: Could all this research eventually extend our human lifespans?

item.title: OpenIndiana Hipster 2026.10 released
item.description: OpenIndiana is a rolling-release illumos distribution, but they do release snapshots twice a year to serve as a base for installations, which they call Hipster. The project’s just released OpenIndiana Hipster 2026.10, and it brings a number of welcome changes. First, there’s UEFI framebuffer support on the live image, which is automatically configured when loading up the image. Second, Firefox and Thunderbird versions have been bumped to 159.0, and a whole slew of development tools have been updated to newer versions as well. This snapshot also brings QEMU 11.1.2 and VirtualBox 7.2.22, and a number of new applications have been added as well. In addition, SPARC build support has been improved to enable new and updated packages for Sun’s dead ISA as well. You can download a fresh image, or update an existing installation through IPS.

As you may be aware, one of the limitations of musl-based distributions is that they will not function to their proper extent when used in computers with various NVIDIA graphics cards. This is due to the proprietary nature of the driver, being built for glibc. I have been experimenting with trying to make this work, and this post is the summary of that effort. ↫ Nina “q66” on the Chimera blog What follows is a deeply technical exploration of the problem, and the steps Nina q66 and the Chimera team are taking to try and fix it. With how popular and widespread NVIDIA hardware still is, this is a hugely important issue to try and address, and I’m grateful they’re trying to address it.

item.title: An ‘Ozempic baby boom’? The GLP-1 pregnancy plot twist
item.description:
The explosion of GLP-1 drugs has created a gray zone for pregnancy. That recently prompted the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists to issue its first ever guidance on the topic. In a twist, the drugs may boost fertility for some, leading to more pregnancies – a phenomenon known on social media as “Ozempic babies”. But doctors caution against using the drugs during pregnancy itself. In fact, the more we looked into this story, the more twists and nuances we found. So, we brought Dr. Amy Valent of Oregon Health and Science University onto the show to break down the latest on what’s known about how these drugs affect fertility and pregnancy.

item.title: MorphOS 3.21 released with new office suite
item.description: About five months after the previous release, the MorphOS team has released MorphOS 3.21. It brings the usual list of big fixes and smaller improvements, but there’s a few big ticket items in here as well. MorphOS 3.21 introduces BasicWorks, an office suite made up of CellBasics and PageBasics. It offers document and spreadsheet authoring and loads and saves Microsoft Office and OpenOffice documents. Also new are NVMEMount, an auto-mounter for booting from and mounting NVMe partitions, and the Marbles and Cyber 3D blankers. Graphics performance has been improved, with a faster Radeon driver on cards with little video memory thanks to GART backed bitmap transfers, quicker TinyGL texture copies, hardware accelerated antialiased text in TTEngine and much faster color SVG glyph rendering in Cairo. The Bcm43xx wireless driver has been substantially reworked, with automatic transmit rate selection, updated firmware and numerous connection fixes. PowerBook and iMac hotkeys are now fully configurable. ↫ MorphOS 3.21 release announcement The BasicWorks office suite has been in the works for a while now, and more information on it can be found in a thread on the MorphZone forums and on the website for the spreadsheet component of the suite, CellBasics. The formula loaders and xlsx loaders are ports of open source projects, but the rest of the application is new code based on ObjectiveC++ and Cairo/Harfbuzz. It uses its own file format, but can import csv and xslsx files, so I’m assuming the same more or else applies to the word processor (but with docx, of course). Alongside MorphOS 3.21 also comes a new release for Wayfarer, the web browser the Amiga-inspired operating system uses. Wayfarer 12.0 moves to WebKitGTK 2.52.5 (which was released in July of 2026, so it’s quite up to date), and now uses the Skia graphics library. R300-R500 Radeons will render websites with Skia-GL for some massive performance improvements, helped further along by a slew of additional performance optimisations. Adblocking has been improved as well, YouTube should work a lot better now, and much more. The full release notes for MorphOS 3.21 give you all the details.

item.title: The port that does not exist
item.description: Ask any program to listen on port 0 and it will hand you a socket on port 47193…or 58037…or whatever the kernel felt like that day. Port 0 is not a port you can have. It is the number you pass when you want the operating system to pick one for you. But a TCP header is just bytes. The destination port field is 16 bits wide, and 0x0000 fits in 16 bits as well as anything else does. Nothing on the wire stops a packet from being addressed to port 0. Your tools will refuse it, your browser will block it, and your scanner’s default port list skips it, because everyone agrees it isn’t a real port. Which makes it a pretty good place to hide things, whether anyone meant to or not. So we did some TCP cowboy shit & port scanned the entire fucking internet for open ports on port 0, which uncovered some interesting unexpected findings. ↫ acidvegas An awesome and entertaining read. Don’t skip this one.

item.title: Windows 11 27H2 might be a more substantial upgrade
item.description: A little tidbit of news regarding the nest major update to Windows, known as Windows 11 27H2. Apparently, it’s going to come with some more serious changes to the codebase, therefore necessitating a full operating system swap instead of a mere enablement package, much like Windows 11 24H2 was. For those who need a refresher, Microsoft has long been rumored to be running on a three-year release cadence and for a while, it was even thought that the company would launch Windows 12 in 2H 2024. That evidently didn’t happen, as instead we got Windows 11 24H2, but it was a major upgrade, a full OS swap compared to Windows 11 23H2 and 22H2. Essentially, it looks like every three releases, Microsoft is performing a full swap with major changes in the underlying codebase, and it seems to line up with Windows 11 27H2 as well. At the moment it’s not known if system requirements will change or not. ↫ Sayan Sen at Neowin.net Microsoft is currently testing adding support for Intel’s Advanced Performance Extensions, which should yield improved 64bit performance and reduced power consumption. It makes sense to assume this support will be coming with Windows 11 27H2, which should hopefully lead to tangible performance improvements across the board. Also, there’s going to be a new default wallpaper. Be still my beating heart.

item.title: The Ubuntu 26.04 Rust sudo is not compatible with standard sudo
item.description: Ubuntu has been at the forefront of replacing the traditional versions of basic tools like sudo with replacements written in Rust, but aside from worries about replacing battle-tested code with brand new, relatively untested code, there’s new things to worry about it. As it turns out, sudo-rs, the Rust replacement for sudo, is intentionally incompatible with the classic version in dangerous ways, as Chris Siebenmann discovered to his dismay. Basically, the classic sudo supports the use of wildcards defined using square brackets, so that if you allow a user to run, say, /usr/sbin/exim -bp, without a password, they can run exim -bpa, exim -bpc, exim -bpr, or exim -bpu without having to supply a password. This allows for very specific, fine-grained access control, which is quite a nice capability to have if you’re managing many systems and users. Sadly, sudo-rs intentionally does not support this, opting to only allow you to use the generic * wildcard. Worse yet, it doesn’t really make this clear, either. ↫ Chris Siebenmann I do not really have words for this. The Rust sudo has apparently opted to keep the single most dangerous wildcard while disallowing all of the wildcards that allow one to be narrow and specific about what you’re allowing, and it buries this at the end of a section that devotes a bunch of words to describing functionality it doesn’t have and doesn’t support, with absolutely nothing else in that section to say this (either up front or in the descriptions of how all the wildcards would work if sudo-rs supported them, which it doesn’t). If you’re going to replace such vital, core tools like sudo that god knows how many people rely on every single day, you better be damn sure you’re feature-complete and can act as a drop-in replacement. If someone switches from sudo to doas, nobody expects the experience to be identical. However, if you’re consistently being told that sudo-rs is a drop-in replacement and you shouldn’t expect any disruptions, you better be able to make true on that promise. Ubuntu isn’t some also-ran small hobby distribution, and its developers should act like it. What a clown show.

item.title: “Why don’t we run the taskbar and Task Manager at high priority, so they can remain responsive?”
item.description: Another interesting post from Raymond Chen, this time about the difficulty of dealing with a system that’s become CPU-starved. The question is simple: why not just run Task Manager and important parts of the UI like the taskbar at a higher priority? The catch with running anything at high priority is that unless you have been very careful to avoid it, you will eventually run into a shared resource that you will have to wait for, and you are now stuck. Your priority checkout pass gets you to the front of the line, but if the person at the register has a large shopping cart full of groceries, you just have to wait until they are done before you get your chance. Even if the code that protects the shared resource is careful to avoid priority inversion by transferring the priority of the waiter to the thread that owns the resource, you are still stuck waiting, and that owning thread might be doing something that takes a long time, like, say, accessing a file over the network. ↫ Raymond Chen If a system has reached a state where even accessing or using something like a task manager becomes a problem, I personally just bonk my computer over the head with a forced shutdown using the power button. Honestly though, I can’t remember the last time I’ve had to do this, as my Linux machines all seem to handle problematic applications just fine. That being said, I’m sure people managing tons of servers and/or workstations and developers debugging their own running code run into catastrophic problems like this far more often, making forced shutdowns not as practical. Have a terminal window open with top and easy access to the kill command, or make sure you can just ssh into it remotely if the UI has gone completely nuts.

item.title: “Jailbreaking my car’s navigation system just so I can change the time”
item.description: What if you want to change the time in your car’s infotainment system, but it’s so locked down that you can’t even open the time settings menu without a very specific, DRM’d SD card? Well, you try to jailbreak it, of course, but the amount of effort required can kind of spiral out of control. And then, all the way at the end, it’s just an offset. The first thing I did was use this to create a full backup of the internal eMMC using dd. With a more complete dump of the system, I pretty quickly figured out that the date & time settings that I’m interested in are in /mnt/flash/settings.dat, which is a custom binary format. After some more reverse engineering, it turned out the unit doesn’t really have a concept of timezones at all. It gets the time from GPS and stores the local offset as a number of minutes. Mine was set to 180. I changed it to 120. That is how I was finally able to fix my car’s timezone. ↫ Rasmus Moorats This harrowing story involved an older car – a 2014 Renault Latitude – but with the number of screens and the amount of user-facing software only increasing every year, requiring jailbreaks to get your car to do what you want it to do are only going to become more common. I wouldn’t be surprised if whole generations of cars are going to become much harder to sell in the near future, cratering the used market, because people are not willing to put up with software problems nobody wants to or can fix. He just wanted to change the goddamn time.

item.title: AI is changing mathematics -- but not how you think
item.description:
Math has created some of humanity's oldest intellectual challenges. And AI is completely changing the game. This year AI solved one of math’s most difficult problems. We get into it with NPR science correspondent Geoff Brumfel, who weighs the risks and rewards of AI’s math takeover.
